newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Thousands pay last respects to Brazilian friar.
newsitem.headline: Thousands pay last respects to Brazilian friar.

text.p: Thousands of Brazilian worshippers wept and sang hymns as they filed past the open coffin of Friar Damiao, a revered monk who died on Saturday, aged 98, officials said.

"People have come by car, by bus and by foot from every corner of the northeast (of Brazil)," said trainee priest Marcilon da Silva by telephone from the Basilica da Penha in the coastal city of Recife.
A line of mourners stretched around several city blocks near the Basilica, da Silva said. A police officer said the crowd numbered several thousand and continued to grow.

"We are certain that at this moment Friar Damiao is showering us with blessings from heaven," Dom Jose Cardoso Sobrinho, archbishop of Olinda and Recife, told national CBN radio. "The poor are beginning to arrive and form never-ending lines to wait patiently for a moment close to Friar Damiao."
Damiao, born Pio Gianotti in 1898 in the Italian city of Bozzano, died on Saturday after his heart and lungs ceased to function. He had been declared brain dead five days earlier.

"Brazil has lost a man who dedicated his life to the poor and the dispossessed," President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said in a statement. "For decades, Friar Damiao brought the message of faith, hope and solidarity to the Brazilian people."
National CBN radio said Cardoso would declare three days of official mourning beginning on Monday.

As a member of the strict Capuchin order, Damiao arrived in Brazil in 1931 and began criss-crossing the vast, arid northeast on foot to preach his fiery sermons to some of Brazil's most remote towns and villages.

He repeatedly said hell was waiting for adulterers, communists, women who used birth control or wore short skirts. In his view, even people who enjoyed to dance, one of the region's favourite pastimes, were damned.
Damiao was banned from preaching in several cities by bishops opposed to his extreme views. But his unflagging drive to bring the Bible to the backlands endeared him to the people.
He was considered by the faithful to be a semi-saint with the power to bring on the rains and save subsistence farmers across the region from starvation.

Old age eventually prevented Damiao from preaching. But helpers continued to bear him through towns and villages where thousands of worshippers would gather in the streets in the hope of kissing his hand or his drooping head.

His body was due to remain in the Basilica until Tuesday when it would be taken to a soccer stadium for a mass expected to be attended by about 100,000 of his followers. The funeral was scheduled for Wednesday.
